justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing level of the S&P 500 around 418–420 at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and typical overnight/intraday noise would keep the index near its recent level with only a small positive drift baked in from the historical equity risk premium. For the one-week estimate, I applied a slightly larger drift to account for a full trading week, while still expecting the index to trade near recent levels absent a major catalyst. The one-month estimate of 428 reflects the compounded effect of that same modest drift, essentially pricing in a roughly 2–2.5% annualized expected return over the period, consistent with near-term equity valuations and a relatively calm macro backdrop at the time.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility of the S&P 500, which in normal regimes runs roughly 15–18% annualized. Translating that into daily, weekly, and monthly standard deviations naturally widens the bands as the horizon extends — from roughly ±11–12 points at one day, to ±22 points at one week, to ±44 points at one month. I also factored in that short-term volatility tends to be somewhat mean-reverting and that macro conditions at the time did not suggest an immediate volatility spike, which kept the one-day interval relatively tight. The one-month interval is wide enough to capture a meaningful range of plausible macro outcomes without being so wide as to be uninformative.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in U.S. economic data — particularly a surprising jump in unemployment claims or a sharp miss in inflation figures — could trigger a rapid risk-off move well below the lower bounds. A renewed escalation in geopolitical tensions, a credit event in a systemically important institution, or an abrupt shift in Federal Reserve communication toward more aggressive tightening could also produce tail outcomes. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish pivot signal from the Fed, or a positive resolution to ongoing trade or geopolitical uncertainties could push the index materially above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for sentiment to shift dramatically in either direction.
